analysis.one_liner: Repeals the individual minimum tax and lets taxpayers elect a flat 10%/25% income tax.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors and no vote: it was introduced in December 2007, placed on the Senate calendar, and died there when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the alternative minimum tax for individuals and let any taxpayer choose, permanently, a simplified income tax with just two rates: 10% on the first $50,000 for singles ($100,000 for couples) and 25% above that, with a large standard deduction and doubled personal exemptions but no itemized deductions or tax credits [S3]. It would also make the reduced 15% tax rate on capital gains and dividends permanent [S2][S3]. Because the alternative is voluntary, people would switch only when it lowered their bill — and the biggest winners would be high earners, who would pay a 25% top rate instead of the regular system's higher brackets and keep the 15% investment rate forever [S3]. The bill never moved beyond the Senate calendar.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income taxpayers gain the most: they could elect a 25% top rate instead of the regular system's top rates, keep the 15% capital gains and dividends rate permanently, and escape the alternative minimum tax [S3][S2]. Middle-income taxpayers who don't itemize would gain a larger standard deduction ($25,000 for couples) and simpler filing [S3]. Anyone who itemizes deductions or claims the earned income or child tax credits could simply stay in the regular system, since the election is optional [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the individual alternative minimum tax for all tax years after 2006, ending a parallel tax that grows to catch more middle-income families each year because it is not indexed to inflation [S2][S3].
Offers a genuinely simpler tax: two rates (10% and 25%), a $25,000 standard deduction for couples, and doubled personal exemptions, replacing the regular system's stacked brackets [S3].
Makes the 15% maximum rate on capital gains and dividends permanent, rather than letting it expire as scheduled [S2][S3].
The choice is voluntary, so no taxpayer would be forced into the alternative system; those who benefit more from the regular system's deductions and credits can decline the election [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury. The bill cuts the top rate to 25%, repeals the minimum tax, and makes the 15% investment rate permanent, with no provision in the text raising revenue to offset any of it [S3]. That shortfall shows up as larger deficits or as higher taxes on someone else later. Within the tax code, families who would elect it lose the child tax credit and earned income tax credit, which the simplified system does not include [S3].

drawbacks.text: The simplified system contains no earned income tax credit or child tax credit, so low- and middle-income families with children would forgo those credits if they elected it, and the election is binding for future years with only a one-time right to revoke [S3].

The bill combines an individual minimum-tax repeal, a 25% top rate, and permanent 15% capital gains and dividends rates with no revenue offset anywhere in its text, meaning the cost would fall on the deficit or on future taxpayers [S3].

The biggest savings go to the highest earners: a taxpayer making several hundred thousand dollars would pay 25% on wages and 15% on investment gains, while the 10% bracket's benefit reaches only the first $50,000 of income for a single filer [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does address two real problems: the minimum tax increasingly snared middle-income families, and the tax code is genuinely too complicated. But its design points the largest benefits at the top. A flat 25% rate plus a permanent 15% rate on investment income cuts the tax bill of a wealthy household far more than the bigger standard deduction helps a typical family, and the simplified option strips out the tax credits that working families rely on. Nothing in the bill pays for itself. An honest reading is that this is a large, permanent tax cut weighted toward high earners, wrapped in a real but secondary simplification benefit.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in early December 2007 and placed on the Senate calendar after two readings, it never got a committee hearing or a floor vote and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Jim DeMint introduced the bill on December 5, 2007; it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 524 [S1][S5].
No committee was assigned, no hearing or markup occurred, and the action history shows nothing after the December 6, 2007 calendar placement [S5].
The bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill's death in a direct sense, because it had not advanced far enough to promise anyone anything. Relative to what the bill offered, high earners and investors lost the chance at a 25% top rate and a permanent 15% capital gains rate, while the Treasury avoided the unoffset revenue loss the bill would have created. Middle-income families' minimum-tax relief had to come from other legislation, since this bill never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury; top earners gained nothing

for.name: Sen. Jim DeMint
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it placed on the Senate calendar; made no further recorded push for it.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor during the 110th Congress; it sat on the calendar until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no one else signed on: a single Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern can be measured.

industries.note: Electing taxpayers would cap their wage tax rate at 25% and lock in a 15% rate on capital gains and dividends, with the minimum tax repealed. Because the election is voluntary and the bill has no revenue offset, the savings come at the cost of larger deficits or future taxes on others.

Making the 15% capital gains and dividends rate permanent removes the scheduled sunset that threatened the after-tax returns the industry sells. Lower rates on investment income chiefly benefit wealthy investors while reducing federal revenue.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: A genuinely simpler two-rate system with a large standard deduction would reduce demand for preparation help among taxpayers who elect it. In practice the regular system would continue alongside it, so the industry keeps most of its business.
